# Trajectories in, improvements out: building a learning machine for search

Agents search differently from people. They send bursts of precise queries, read every result in full, and decide from the text alone whether to search again, open a page or answer. Each run leaves a trajectory: what the agent asked, what Keenable returned, what it opened and how many tokens it spent. Those trajectories show failures that no per-query metric can, so we built a system that learns from them.

We call it a learning machine. Agents read the trajectories, find where search failed the agent, write up the cause, then design, run and evaluate the fixes. People decide which of those failures matter and approve what ships. This post walks through how the loop works and one problem it fixed over four production releases (Figure 1).

Figure 1. The learning machine. Agents read the trajectories and report where search failed, and people pick which problem is worth a round. Agents then test ideas in quick 40-step runs, send the promising ones to full training and an online evaluation on live queries, and a person approves what ships. Each release serves the traffic the next round learns from. Run counts cover the four host-quality rounds and are illustrative.

## A weak result costs an agent more than one query

Search quality is usually measured one query at a time: take the ranked list for a query and grade it against relevance labels. Our own benchmark, NEEDLE [1] , works that way, and it still tells us whether a single result list is good. It canât tell us what happens over a whole agent run.

Agents also donât search like the people those metrics were built around. Their queries are longer and packed with quoted phrases, site: filters and dates, and they arrive in bursts, each one rewritten from what the last results said [4] (Figure 2). The NEEDLE post covers why that breaks engines tuned for human clicks. For this post, one consequence matters: an agentâs next query depends on what our last result told it.

Figure 2. Queries people typed into AOL search in 2006 next to a sample of queries agents sent to Keenable: their median length, which features they contain, and their most frequent words.

So an agent run is a chain, and a weak link costs more than one query. When results are long or only half relevant, the agent searches again, opens more pages and rereads a longer context before it answers. Two runs of the same task with the same model can both end with the right answer while one reads several times as many tokens. Judged query by query, the two runs look alike. The difference only shows up across the whole trajectory.

Nobody had to report these failures to us. They were in our own logs: on some kinds of tasks, agents using Keenable needed more searches, more fetches and more tokens to reach an answer. That is where the learning machine starts.

## Every day, analysis agents turn trajectories into failure reports

A trajectory is the full record of an agent run as Keenable sees it: every query with its operators, the results and snippet text we returned, the rankerâs score for every candidate, which results the agent fetched and how many tokens it read. We collect them from production traffic and from evaluation runs, where we also know whether the final answer was right.

Nobody can review them by hand. An agentâs query is written by a machine, for a machine, partway through a task the reader canât see, and there are millions of them. So analysis agents read the previous dayâs trajectories every day. They group them by kind of task and compare what agents searched for, which results they fetched, which they cited and how many tokens they spent. Fetches are the closest thing agents give us to a click: when agents in one cluster keep skipping the top results to open something ranked seventh, that is a ranking failure no relevance label will show.

Each pattern becomes a short report with the evidence, a hypothesis and the stage of the stack it suspects: crawl, retrieval, ranking, snippets or fetch (Figure 3). People read the reports and decide which ones are worth a round of fixing.

Figure 3. The shape of a report from the daily trajectory analysis, for one cluster of finance tasks. Illustrative example; the numbers are not measured values.

## Agents skipped our top results to reach better sources

Two patterns stood out early, and neither shows up in a per-query metric.

Right page, wrong snippet. Our snippets used to come from the top of each page, but on long documents the answer usually sits further down. Agents either answered without it or fetched the whole document. Dynamic snippets now pull the spans that match the query from anywhere in the page. After the August 30 rollout, the mean search response in production fell from 135 KiB to 69 KiB. The details are in the Dynamic Snippets post [5] .

The best source ranked too low. In finance tasks, agents kept skipping our top results to open pages further down on more authoritative hosts: the 10-K on sec.gov instead of a portalâs summary of it. Our relevance judge labels each resultâs host as preferred, acceptable or unsuitable for the kind of query, and we track host quality, the share of relevant top results that come from preferred hosts. On relevance, Keenable was the best engine we measured. On host quality it was the worst: 46 to 55% of our relevant top-five results came from preferred hosts, against 67 to 73% for the other engines. The agents had been routing around our ranking to reach the better sources. The rest of this post follows that one problem through the loop.

## Most ideas stop after 40 training steps. Four shipped.

Once people pick a report, agents run the round. They trace the cause, compute how much there is to gain, design training changes, run them, evaluate them and check that nothing else regressed. It is closer to AlphaEvolve [6] than to a system that redesigns itself: agents propose many changes, metrics decide which ones survive, and people approve what ships.

Every change goes through the same funnel. A quick run trains for 40 steps, enough to see whether a change moves the offline metrics. Promising changes get full training and a full offline evaluation. The best go to an online evaluation on live queries, and one ships. Most ideas die in the first stage, which is the point: a quick run is cheap enough that an agent can try an idea it isnât sure about, and the expensive stages only see what survived. For host quality, that meant hundreds of quick runs and four releases (Figure 4).

Figure 4. Every training run the agents launched for host quality, one dot per run, colored by the stage where it stopped. Illustrative counts.

Which host is authoritative depends on the query: the SEC filing for a companyâs reported numbers, the regulator for the maximum dose of a drug, the projectâs own documentation for a software setting. So the judge labels hosts per kind of query. Preferred is the source an expert would cite, acceptable is a reliable secondary source, and unsuitable covers copies, content farms and spam.

Round 1, released October 10: find the bug. An agent audited why the ranker ignored source quality. The host label was there for every training example, but the training target threw it away: it only capped unsuitable hosts, which changed 0.5% of training pairs. The fix was a target that shifts each pageâs grade up or down by its host label. In production, the share of preferred hosts rose 5 points, and relevance rose too.

The ceiling. Before tuning that shift, the agent computed what a perfect reranker could do with the same candidates: 2,550 queries and 316,000 graded candidates, reordered four ways (Figure 5). Sorting perfectly by relevance does nothing for host quality. Putting preferred hosts first wins host quality at a large cost in relevance. Ordering by relevance and breaking ties with the host label reaches 0.788 host quality with no loss of relevance at all. All of the room is in how near-ties are broken, and the round-1 target, even learned perfectly, reached only about half of it.

Figure 5. The ceiling, computed before any training: the same candidates reordered four ways, scored on relevance and host quality. 2,550 queries, 316,000 graded candidates.

Round 2, released October 20: the dial. The agent swept the size of the host shift across ten settings, from Â±0.3 to Â±1.5, one quick run each. Host quality rose with every step; relevance fell slowly at first and faster past Â±1.0. Offline, Â±1.0 looked like the best trade, and it was chosen on October 17. A 500-query online evaluation the same day showed relevance down a full point, so the choice went back to Â±0.6 before it reached production (Figure 6). The release went out with host quality up 3 points and relevance flat. The lesson was about the metrics: a relevance loss that looks negligible offline can be visible online.

Figure 6. Round 2. The agent tested ten sizes of the host shift, from Â±0.3 to Â±1.5. Â±1.0 won offline and was chosen on October 17, then reverted the same day when a 500-query online evaluation showed relevance down a point. Â±0.6 shipped on October 20 with host quality up 3 points and relevance flat.

Round 3, released October 28: relevance first. Round 3 changed the target so that relevance always comes first: a relevant page always outranks an irrelevant one, and the host label only decides the order among pages that are equally relevant. That is exactly where the ceiling said the room was. On 1,000 paired queries, host quality rose 8 points and relevance rose with it.

Round 4, released November 10: one source, not three. With round 3 live, the analysis agents went back to the trajectories and found the next pattern: agents opening the same text two or three times, once on the original host and again on mirrors and scraped copies. A copy of a relevant page is just as relevant, so copies kept their slots in the top ten. Round 4 taught the ranker to keep the original and rank its copies below it. On 1,000 paired queries, copies fell from 4% to 1.5% of top-ten slots, host quality rose 2 points, and relevance held. That pattern only existed in the trajectories of the model round 3 produced. Every release changes what the next analysis sees.

On our host-quality board (Figure 7), Keenable started at 64.4% on October 15, below every engine shown. Round 2 barely moved the line. After round 3 it rose for a week as the seven-day mean filled with days on the new model and passed Perplexity. After round 4 it passed Brave and then Exa, and reached 78.9% on November 17.

Figure 7. Host quality on a fixed query set, October 15 to November 17, 2026, as a 7-day rolling mean. Other engines are shown at their November 17 values. Round 1 shipped on October 10, before the board starts.

Agents will reward hack if you let them. An agent optimizing a metric will use whatever data improves it, and in the first round-3 attempt that meant last weekâs evaluation queries. Training on the eval set would have made the round look better offline without making search any better. A person caught it within minutes, the training table was rebuilt from the training stream alone, and evaluation data is now kept out of the agentsâ reach.

## The same loop has shipped 93 parser fixes since June

The reports don't only point at the ranker. They also name crawl, retrieval, snippets and fetch, and the same loop applies at each stage. Content parsing is where it has shipped the most fixes so far.

How a parsing round runs. Every night the loop samples a day of URLs and has a cheap judge grade our current extraction of each page. It keeps about 500 pages judged bad, plus 500 judged good as a regression cohort. A stronger model then marks up a reference version of every page.
